Data-driven accelerated multigrid method for Riesz space fractional diffusion equations **Abstract** The multigrid method is one of the most efficient iterative methods for solving large structured linear systems, and its efficiency stems from the complementarity between the smoother and the coarse grid correction. In this paper, we consider the block Toeplitz linear system obtained by discretizing time dependent Riesz space fractional diffusion equations, and employ the weighted Jacobi iterative method as a smoother. The weighted Jacobi smoother features a simple structure and low computational cost, yet its smoothing property is highly dependent on the relaxation parameter. We adopt Gaussian process regression to select the relaxation parameter to accelerate the convergence of the multigrid method. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical analysis, which simultaneously verifies the effectiveness and superiority of the data-driven parameter selection strategy. **Keywords:** Multigrid methods, Fractional differential equations, Gaussian process regression ## 1. Introduction Fractional differential equations are powerful mathematical tools that can accurately describe certain complex phenomena, such as pricing options [1, 17], control problems [10, 23], image processing [4, 2]. Consider a two-dimensional Riesz space fractional diffusion equation as follows: \(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } d(x,y,t)\frac{\partial u(x,y,t)}{\partial t}-\frac{\partial^{\gamma_1}u(x,y,t)}{\partial|x|^{\gamma_1}}-\frac{\partial^{\gamma_2}u(x,y,t)}{\partial|y|^{\gamma_2}}=f(x,y,t), & (x,y,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T), \\ u(x,y,t)=0, & (x,y,t)\in\partial\Omega\times(0,T), \\ u(x,y,0)=u_0(x,y), & (x,y)\in\bar{\Omega}, \end{array}\right.\) (1.1) where \(\Omega=(x_L,x_R)\times(y_L,y_R)\), \(\partial\Omega\) denotes the boundary of \(\Omega\), _f(x,y,t_) is the source term, \(d(x,y,t)\ge 0\) is the coefficient function. _u_0(_x,y_) is the initial condition, \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in(1,2)\). Specifically, Riesz fractional derivatives are defined as follows: \(\frac{\partial^{\gamma_1}u(x,y,t)}{\partial|x|^{\gamma_1}}=\sigma_{\gamma_1}\left(x_LD_x^{\gamma_1}+_xD_{x_R}^{\gamma_1}\right)u(x,y,t),\)
\(\frac{\partial^{\gamma_2}u(x,y,t)}{\partial|y|^{\gamma_2}}=\sigma_{\gamma_2}\left(y_LD_y^{\gamma_2}+_yD_{y_R}^{\gamma_2}\right)u(x,y,t),\) _Email address:_ `zhangjuan@xtu.edu.cn` ( Juan Zhang∗1,2) Yang Hu1, Juan Zhang∗1,2 1 School of Mathematics and Computational Science, Xiangtan University, Xiangtan, 411105, Hunan, People’s Republic of China 2 Hunan Key Laboratory for Computation and Simulation in Science and Engineering, Xiangtan University, Xiangtan, People’s Republic of China

with \(\sigma_{\gamma_l}=-\frac{1}{2cos(\pi\gamma_l/2)}>0\) for _l_=1,2. Owing to the nonlocality of fractional differential operators, it is difficult to obtain the analytical solutions of fractional differential equations, and thus developing efficient numerical methods to acquire their numerical solutions has become a research focus in this field.

Discretizing equation (1.1) on a uniform grid using the shifted Grünwald difference scheme in space and the backward Euler scheme in time yields a sequence of Toeplitz-like linear systems. Due to the nonlocality of fractional differential operators, the coefficient matrices are generally dense, which renders the discrete linear systems computationally expensive for general purpose solvers. For solving such linear systems, [5] proposed a class of diagonal-Toeplitz splitting (DTS) iteration methods, implemented by alternately solving shifted diagonal and shifted Toeplitz subsystems. Building upon the DTS framework, [16] used a natural \(\tau\) approximation of the symmetric Toeplitz component and proposed a sine-transform-based splitting preconditioner. More recently, [26] decomposed the coefficient matrix by extracting a scalar matrix, a diagonal compensation matrix, and a block \(\tau\) matrix. The sum of these matrices was then employed to construct a class of \(\tau\)-splitting iteration methods.

For certain structured matrices, the multigrid method exhibits excellent solution efficiency[24, 15, 6]. Under suitable conditions, this method enjoys mesh-independent convergence. This advantageous property has drawn the attention of many researchers to investigate the application of multigrid methods to fractional partial differential equations. For instance, [21] employed the two-grid method to solve the dense Toeplitz linear system obtained after discretizing the one-dimensional constant-coefficient fractional diffusion equation, and utilized fast Toeplitz matrix-vector multiplication to reduce the computational overhead . [9] proved the convergence of the multigrid method for two-dimensional space-fractional diffusion equations with constant diffusion coefficients. Based on the generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) sequences theory, they further extended this result to the case of uniformly bounded and positive variable diffusion coefficients. Furthermore, numerous studies adopt the GLT theory to analyze the spectral properties of coefficient matrices and thereby design multigrid methods[2, 25, 3]. In addition, [7, 8] extended the symbol-based multigrid analysis for scalar Toeplitz matrices to block-circulant and block-Toeplitz systems generated by matrix-valued symbols, and derived sufficient conditions for the two- grid and V-cycle methods .

The multigrid method consists of a smoother and a coarse-grid correction that complement each other. The coarse-grid correction is responsible for eliminating the low-frequency components of the error. For Toeplitz-like matrices, coarse-grid correction using bilinear interpolation as the transfer operator is effective and general [20]. Correspondingly, the smoother should rapidly attenuate the high-frequency components of the error that are difficult for the coarse grid to represent, and it is usually implemented by classical iterative methods. The weighted Jacobi method is widely adopted due to its simplicity and low computational cost per iteration. With an appropriate relaxation parameter, this method exhibits favorable smoothing ability for high-frequency components of the error[30, 32]. Therefore, the proper choice of the relaxation parameter is the key to constructing an efficient smoother.

Previously, research on the selection of relaxation parameters for the weighted Jacobi smoother has mainly focused on classical elliptic partial differential equations[12, 13]. [3]extended this study to dense Toeplitz- type linear systems arising from the discretization of tempered fractional diffusion equations. They used the spectral information provided by the generating function of the coefficient matrix to expand the range of parameters that guarantee the smoothing property of the Jacobi smoother, and gave estimation formulas for suitable relaxation parameters. However, while their estimation formulas yield feasible relaxation parameters, the resulting parameter may not always match the numerically optimal choice for finite-dimensional linear systems.

In recent years, the integration of machine learning with traditional numerical methods has demonstrated great potential. Machine learning techniques can identify nonlinear relationships between problem characteristics and numerical algorithms from data that are difficult to characterize explicitly, thereby providing new approaches to the design of complex numerical algorithms and the automatic selection of their parameters. Moreover, once trained, machine learning models can typically make rapid predictions for new problems at a low computational cost. In the field of multigrid methods, [11, 33, 31] have applied machine learning to the<tbc>

design and optimization of smoothers. In this work, we adopt Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) to learn and select the relaxation parameters of the weighted Jacobi smoother, so as to improve the convergence speed of the multigrid method. GPR is a Bayesian nonparametric learning method that places a Gaussian process prior on the unknown mapping from problem features to the desired relaxation parameter. Given a small set of training samples, the correlations among the samples are characterized by a covariance kernel, and conditioning the prior on the observed data yields a posterior predictive distribution for a new problem instance. Its mean can be used as the predicted relaxation parameter, while its variance provides a quantitative measure of prediction uncertainty. It can capture nonlinear parameter dependence without prescribing a fixed functional form, perform well with relatively small datasets, and, once trained, deliver predictions at a low online cost. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2,we discretize the original equations and analyze the basic spectral properties of the coefficient matrix. In Section 3, with the aid of the Ruge-Stuben two grid framework, we design and analyze the convergence of the two grid method. In Section 4, we introduce the principles of GPR and its procedure for predicting parameters. In Section 5, we present numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the multigrid method and GPR for parameter prediction. In Section 6, we summarize the conclusions and future work. ## 2. Discretization and matrix properties In this section, we will introduce the specific discrete schemes and analyze the properties of the coefficient matrices obtained from the discretization, which will help us design the multigrid method. Below, we review the left- and right-sided Riemann-Liouville fractional derivatives: \(x_LD_x^{\gamma_1}u(x,y,t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(2-\gamma_1)}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\int_{x_L}^x\frac{u(\xi,y,t)}{(x-\xi)^{\gamma_1-1}}d\xi,x_D_{x_R}^{\gamma_1}u(x,y,t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(2-\gamma_1)}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\int_x^{x_R}\frac{u(\xi,y,t)}{(\xi-x)^{\gamma_1-1}}d\xi,\)
\(y_LD_y^{\gamma_2}u(x,y,t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(2-\gamma_2)}\frac{d^2}{dy^2}\int_{y_L}^y\frac{u(x,\xi,t)}{(y-\xi)^{\gamma_2-1}}d\xi,y_D_{y_R}^{\gamma_2}u(x,y,t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(2-\gamma_2)}\frac{d^2}{dy^2}\int_y^{y_R}\frac{u(x,\xi,t)}{(\xi-y)^{\gamma_2-1}}d\xi,\) where \(\Gamma(\cdot)\) is the Gamma function. Let _N,M_ be positive integers. Take the step sizes \(\Delta x=\frac{x_R-x_L}{N+1}\) , \(\Delta y=\frac{y_R-y_L}{N+1}\) , \(\Delta t=\frac{T}{M}\) to discretize the _x_-direction, _y_-direction and time, yielding \(\{x_i|x_i=x_L+i\Delta x,0\le i\le N+1\},\)
\(\{y_j|y_j=y_L+j\Delta y,0\le j\le N+1\},\)
\(\{t_m|t_m=m\Delta t,0\le m\le M\}.\) Define \(u_{i,j}^{(m)}=u(x_i,y_j,t_m)\), \(f_{i,j}^{(m)}=f(x_i,y_j,t_m)\), \(d_{i,j}^{(m)}=d(x_i,y_j,t_m)\). Using the shifted Grünwald formula\[19, 18\], we can obtain the approximation of the fractional derivative at the point (_xi,yj,tm_): \(x_LD_x^{\gamma_1}(x_i,y_j,t_m)=\frac{1}{\Delta x^{\gamma_1}}\sum_{k=0}^{i+1}g_k^{(\gamma_1)}u_{i-k+1,j}^{(m)}+\mathcal{O}(\Delta x),\)
\(x_D_{x_R}^{\gamma_1}(x_i,y_j,t_m)=\frac{1}{\Delta x^{\gamma_1}}\sum_{k=0}^{N-i+2}g_k^{(\gamma_1)}u_{i+k-1,j}^{(m)}+\mathcal{O}(\Delta x),\) and \(y_LD_y^{\gamma_2}(x_i,y_j,t_m)=\frac{1}{\Delta_y^{\gamma_2}}\sum_{k=0}^{j+1}g_k^{(\gamma_2)}u_{i,j-k+1}^{(m)}+\mathcal{O}(\Delta y),\)
\(y_D_{y_R}^{\gamma_2}(x_i,y_j,t_m)=\frac{1}{\Delta_y^{\gamma_2}}\sum_{k=0}^{N-j+2}g_k^{(\gamma_2)}u_{i,j+k-1}^{(m)}+\mathcal{O}(\Delta y),\)

where the coefficients \(g_k^{(\gamma)}\) are given by the following lemma: **Lemma 2.1.** \[16\] For \(\gamma\in(1,2)\), the following recurrence relation holds: \(g_k^{(\gamma)}=\left(1-\frac{\gamma+1}{k}\right)g_{k-1}^{(\gamma)}=\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}\gamma(\gamma-1)\cdots(\gamma-k+1),k=1,2,\cdots.\) Moreover, we have \(g_0^{(\gamma)}=1,g_1^{(\gamma)}=-\gamma<0,1>g_2^{(\gamma)}>g_3^{(\gamma)}>\cdots>0,\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty g_k^{(\gamma)}=0,\text{or equivalently,}\gamma=\sum_{k=0k\neq 1}^\infty g_k^{(\gamma)}.\) To facilitate the subsequent analysis, we introduce a matrix \(T_N^\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) associated with \(\gamma\): \(T_N^\gamma=-\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c } 2g_1^{(\gamma)} & g_0^{(\gamma)}+g_2^{(\gamma)} & g_3^{(\gamma)} & \cdots & g_{N-1}^{(\gamma)} & g_N^{(\gamma)} \\ g_0^{(\gamma)}+g_2^{(\gamma)} & 2g_1^{(\gamma)} & g_0^{(\gamma)}+g_2^{(\gamma)} & \ddots & \cdots & g_{N-1}^{(\gamma)} \\ g_3^{(\gamma)} & g_0^{(\gamma)}+g_2^{(\gamma)} & 2g_1^{(\gamma)} & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & g_3^{(\gamma)} \\ g_{N-1}^{(\gamma)} & \cdots & \ddots & \ddots & 2g_1^{(\gamma)} & g_0^{(\gamma)}+g_2^{(\gamma)} \\ g_N^{(\gamma)} & g_{N-1}^{(\gamma)} & \cdots & g_3^{(\gamma)} & g_0^{(\gamma)}+g_2^{(\gamma)} & 2g_1^{(\gamma)} \end{array}\right].\) (2.1) According to Lemma 2.1, \(T_N^\gamma\) is a matrix that is strictly diagonally dominant, symmetric, and has all positive diagonal entries. Therefore, \(T_N^\gamma\) is a symmetric positive definite matrix. Let \(\mathbf{u}^{(m)}=[u_{1,1}^{(m)},u_{2,1}^{(m)},\dots,u_{N,1}^{(m)},u_{1,2}^{(m)},u_{2,2}^{(m)},\dots,u_{N,2}^{(m)},\dots,u_{1,N}^{(m)},u_{2,N}^{(m)},\dots,u_{N,N}^{(m)}]^T,\)
\(\mathbf{f}^{(m)}=[f_{1,1}^{(m)},f_{2,1}^{(m)},\dots,f_{N,1}^{(m)},f_{1,2}^{(m)},f_{2,2}^{(m)},\dots,f_{N,2}^{(m)},\dots,f_{1,N}^{(m)},f_{2,N}^{(m)},\dots,f_{N,N}^{(m)}]^T,\)
\(D^{(m)}=\text{diag}(d_{1,1}^{(m)},d_{2,1}^{(m)},\dots,d_{N,1}^{(m)},d_{1,2}^{(m)},d_{2,2}^{(m)},\dots,d_{N,2}^{(m)},\dots,d_{1,N}^{(m)},d_{2,N}^{(m)},\dots,d_{N,N}^{(m)}).\) We discretize (1.1) in the spatial direction using the shifted Grunwald formula and in the temporal direction using the backward Euler scheme to obtain the implicit finite-difference scheme: \(d_{i,j}^{(m)}\frac{u_{i,j}^{(m)}-u_{i,j}^{(m-1)}}{\Delta t}-\frac{\sigma_{\gamma_1}}{\Delta x^{\gamma_1}}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{i+1}g_k^{(\gamma_1)}u_{i-k+1,j}^{(m)}+\sum_{k=0}^{N-i+2}g_k^{(\gamma_1)}u_{i+k-1,j}^{(m)}\right)-\frac{\sigma_{\gamma_2}}{\Delta y^{\gamma_2}}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{j+1}g_k^{(\gamma_2)}u_{i,j-k+1}^{(m)}+\sum_{k=0}^{N-j+2}g_k^{(\gamma_2)}u_{i,j+k-1}^{(m)}\right)=f_{i,j}^{(m)}.\) Furthermore, we have \(D^{(m)}\frac{\mathbf{u}^{(m)}-\mathbf{u}^{(m-1)}}{\Delta t}+\left(\frac{\sigma_{\gamma_1}}{\Delta x^{\gamma_1}}I_N\otimes T_{\gamma_1}+\frac{\sigma_{\gamma_2}}{\Delta y^{\gamma_2}}T_{\gamma_2}\otimes I_N\right)\mathbf{u}^{(m)}=\mathbf{f}^{(m)}.\) Let \(\eta_1=\sigma_{\gamma_1}\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x^{\gamma_1}},\eta_2=\sigma_{\gamma_2}\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta y^{\gamma_2}}\) . Consequently, we obtain \(\left(D^{(m)}+\eta_1I_N\otimes T_N^{\gamma_1}+\eta_2T_N^{\gamma_2}\otimes I_N\right)\mathbf{u}^{(m)}=\Delta t\mathbf{f}^{(m)}+D^{(m)}\mathbf{u}^{(m-1)}.\) (2.2)

Dividing both sides of (2.2) by \(\eta_1\), we have \(\left(\frac{1}{\eta_1}D^{(m)}+I_N\otimes T_N^{\gamma_1}+\frac{\eta_2}{\eta_1}T_N^{\gamma_2}\otimes I_N\right)\mathbf{u}^{(m)}=\frac{1}{\eta_1}\Delta t\mathbf{f}^{(m)}+\frac{1}{\eta_1}D^{(m)}\mathbf{u}^{(m-1)}.\) Define \(A_N^{(m)}=\frac{1}{\eta_1}D^{(m)}+I_N\otimes T_N^{\gamma_1}+\frac{\eta_2}{\eta_1}T_N^{\gamma_2}\otimes I_N,\)
\(\mathbf{b}^{(m)}=\frac{1}{\eta_1}\Delta t\mathbf{f}^{(m)}+\frac{1}{\eta_1}D^{(m)}\mathbf{u}^{(m-1)}.\) (2.3) Then (2.2) is equivalent to \(A_N^{(m)}\mathbf{u}^{(m)}=\mathbf{b}^{(m)},1\le m\le M.\) (2.4) After fixing the partition number _N_, discretizing (1.1) yields a set of matrices \(\{A_N^{(m)}\}\). When the coefficient _d(x,y,t_)=0, _D_(_m_) degenerates to the zero matrix, and in this case, \(A_N^{(m)}\) is independent of the time level _m_ and is denoted by _AN_. The matrix _AN_ is symmetric positive definite and strictly diagonally dominant, and it is a Block-Toeplitz-Toeplitz-Block (BTTB) matrix. BTTB matrices belong to the class of multilevel Toeplitz matrices, and their spectral information is closely related to the generating function of the corresponding BTTB matrix sequence. Let us now recall the definitions of Toeplitz matrix sequences and BTTB matrix sequences. **Definition 2.1.** \[20\] Let \(f(\theta)\in L^1([-\pi,\pi])\) and let {_fk_} be the Fourier coefficients defined as \(f_k:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[-\pi,\pi]}f(\theta)e^{-\mathbf{i}k\theta}\mathrm{d}\theta,\) where **i**2=-1. Then the Toeplitz matrix of order _n_ associated with \(f(\theta)\) is \(T_n(f)=[f_{i-j}]_{i,j=1}^n.\) The function \(f(\theta)\) is called the generating function of the matrix sequence \(\{T_n(f)\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\). **Definition 2.2.** \[20\] Let \(f(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in L^1([-\pi,\pi]^2)\) and let {_f_\[_k_1_,k_2\]} be the Fourier coefficients defined as \(f_{[k_1,k_2]}=\frac{1}{4\pi^2}\int_{-\pi}^\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi f(\theta_1,\theta_2)e^{-\mathbf{i}(k_1\theta_1+k_2\theta_2)}\mathrm{d}\theta_1\mathrm{d}\theta_2.\) Then the Block-Toeplitz-Toeplitz-Blocks matrix of order _n=n_1_n_2 associated with \(f(\theta_1,\theta_2)\) is \(T_n^{(2)}(f)=\left[\left[f_{[i_1-j_1,i_2-j_2]}\right]_{i_2,j_2=1}^{n_2}\right]_{i_1,j_1=1}^{n_1}.\) Accordingly, \(f(\theta_1,\theta_2)\) is called the generating function of matrix sequence \(\{T_n^{(2)}(f)\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\). **Lemma 2.2.** \[22, 9\] Let \(\gamma\in(1,2)\). The generating function of \(\{T_N^\gamma\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\) in (2.1) is real-valued and even, and its specific form is as follows: \(f_\gamma(\theta)=-2^{\gamma+1}(\mathrm{sin}\frac{|\theta|}{2})^\gamma\mathrm{cos}(|\theta|(1-\frac{\gamma}{2})+\frac{\gamma\pi}{2}).\) (2.6) _Proof._ It is noted that the generating function of \(\{T_N^\gamma\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\) is \(f_\gamma(\theta)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^\infty f_ke^{\mathbf{i}k\theta},\) where the coefficients are given by \(f_0=-2g_1^{(\gamma)},f_1=f_{-1}=-g_0^{(\gamma)}-g_2^{(\gamma)},f_k=f_{-k}=-g_{k+1}^{(\gamma)},k\ge 2.\) Furthermore, we obtain that \(\sum_{k=-\infty}^\infty f_ke^{\mathbf{i}k\theta}=-\sum_{k=-1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\gamma)}e^{\mathbf{i}k\theta}-\sum_{k=-1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\gamma)}e^{-\mathbf{i}k\theta}.\) By virtue of the results in \[9\], we have \(-\sum_{k=-1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\gamma)}e^{\mathbf{i}k\theta}=-e^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}(1-e^{\mathbf{i}\theta})^\gamma,\) and \(-\sum_{k=-1}^\infty g_{k+1}^{(\gamma)}e^{-\mathbf{i}k\theta}=-e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}(1-e^{-\mathbf{i}\theta})^\gamma.\) Owing to \(1-e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } 2\left|\mathrm{sin}\frac{\theta}{2}\right|e^{\frac{1}{2}(\theta-\pi)}, & 0\le\theta\le\pi, \\ 2\left|\mathrm{sin}\frac{\theta}{2}\right|e^{\frac{1}{2}(\theta+\pi)}, & -\pi\le\theta<0, \end{array}\right.\text{and}1-e^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } 2\left|\mathrm{sin}\frac{\theta}{2}\right|e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\theta-\pi)}, & 0\le\theta\le\pi, \\ 2\left|\mathrm{sin}\frac{\theta}{2}\right|e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\theta+\pi)}, & -\pi\le\theta<0. \end{array}\right.\) When \(0\le\theta\le\pi\), \(f_\gamma(\theta)=-e^{-\mathbf{i}\theta}(1-e^{\mathbf{i}\theta})^\gamma-e^{\mathbf{i}\theta}(1-e^{-\mathbf{i}\theta})^\gamma\)
\(=-e^{-\mathbf{i}\theta} 2^\gamma\left|\mathrm{sin}^\gamma\frac{\theta}{2}\right|e^{\frac{\mathrm{i}\gamma}{2}(\theta-\pi)}-e^{\mathbf{i}\theta} 2^\gamma\left|\mathrm{sin}^\gamma\frac{\theta}{2}\right|e^{\frac{-\mathrm{i}\gamma}{2}(\theta-\pi)}\)
\(=-2^\gamma\left|\mathrm{sin}^\gamma\frac{\theta}{2}\right|\left(e^{\mathbf{i}\left(\theta(\frac{\gamma}{2}-1)-\frac{\pi\gamma}{2}\right)}+e^{\mathbf{i}\left(-\theta(\frac{\gamma}{2}-1)+\frac{\pi\gamma}{2}\right)}\right)\)
\(=-2^{\gamma+1}\left|\mathrm{sin}^\gamma\frac{\theta}{2}\right|\mathrm{cos}\left(\theta(1-\frac{\gamma}{2})+\frac{\pi\gamma}{2}\right).\) When \(-\pi<\theta\le 0\), \(f_\gamma(\theta)=-2^\gamma\left|\mathrm{sin}^\gamma\frac{\theta}{2}\right|\left(e^{\mathbf{i}\left(\theta(\frac{\gamma}{2}-1)+\frac{\pi\gamma}{2}\right)}+e^{\mathbf{i}\left(-\theta(\frac{\gamma}{2}-1)-\frac{\pi\gamma}{2}\right)}\right)\)
\(=-2^{\gamma+1}\left|\mathrm{sin}^\gamma\frac{\theta}{2}\right|\mathrm{cos}\left(-\theta(1-\frac{\gamma}{2})+\frac{\pi\gamma}{2}\right).\)

Combining the two gives (2.6).
The Proof is completed. With the above preparations, we obtain the generating function of the BTTB matrix sequence \(\{A_N\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\). **Theorem 2.1.** Let \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in(1,2)\). Then _AN_ is the BTTB matrix given by \(A_N=T_n^{(2)}(f_{\gamma_1,\gamma_2})\) with \(f_{\gamma_1,\gamma_2}(\theta_1,\theta_2)=f_{\gamma_1}(\theta_1)+\frac{\eta_2}{\eta_1}f_{\gamma_2}(\theta_2),\) (2.7) where \(\eta_1=\sigma_{\gamma_1}\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x^{\gamma_1}},\eta_2=\sigma_{\gamma_2}\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta y^{\gamma_2}}\) , and \(f_\gamma(\theta)\) is defined in (2.6). _Proof._ By the definition of _AN_, we have \(A_N=I_N\otimes T_{\gamma_1}+\frac{\eta_2}{\eta_1}T_{\gamma_2}\otimes I_N,\) where \(I_N\otimes T_{\gamma_1}=T_N(1)\otimes T_N(f_{\gamma_1})=T_n^{(2)}(\widetilde{f}_{\gamma_1}),\)
\(T_{\gamma_2}\otimes I_N=T_N(f_{\gamma_2})\otimes T_N(1)=T_n^{(2)}(\widetilde{f}_{\gamma_2}).\) Moreover, the Fourier coefficients of \(\widetilde{f}_{\gamma_1}\) and \(\widetilde{f}_{\gamma_2}\) are given by \(\left(\widetilde{f}_{\gamma_1}\right)_{[k_1,k_2]}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } (f_{\gamma_1})_{k_1}, & k_2=0, \\ 0, & k_2\neq 0, \end{array}\right.\text{and}\left(\widetilde{f}_{\gamma_2}\right)_{[k_1,k_2]}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } (f_{\gamma_2})_{k_2}, & k_1=0, \\ 0, & k_1\neq 0. \end{array}\right.\) Hence, \(\widetilde{f}_{\gamma_1}(\theta_1,\theta_2)=f_{\gamma_1}(\theta_1)\) and \(\widetilde{f}_{\gamma_2}(\theta_1,\theta_2)=f_{\gamma_2}(\theta_2)\). Therefore, the generating function of \(\{A_N\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\) is \(f_{\gamma_1,\gamma_2}(\theta_1,\theta_2)=f_{\gamma_1}(\theta_1)+\frac{\eta_2}{\eta_1}f_{\gamma_2}(\theta_2).\) The proof is completed. **Remark 2.1.** If a bivariate function \(f(\theta_1,\theta_2)\) satisfies \(f(\theta_1,\theta_2)=f(|\theta_1|,|\theta_2|)\), then \(f(\theta_1,\theta_2)\) is called an even function. It is easy to verify that \(f_{\gamma_1,\gamma_2}(\theta_1,\theta_2)\) is a bivariate continuous real-valued even function. For a real-valued continuous even function \(f(\theta_1,\theta_2)\), the associated BTTB matrix \(T_n^{(2)}(f)\) is real symmetric. To characterize the spectrum of the matrices generated by \(f_{\gamma_1,\gamma_2}(\theta_1,\theta_2)\), we recall the following standard result, which bounds the eigenvalues in terms of the minimum and maximum of the generating function: **Lemma 2.3.** \[28\] Let \(f(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in C^1([-\pi,\pi]^2)\) be a real-valued even function , with its maximum and minimum denoted by _f_max and _f_min, respectively. Then \(T_n^{(2)}(f)\) is a real symmetric matrix, and its eigenvalues are bounded by the range of \(f(\theta_1,\theta_2)\) in the sense that \(f_\mathrm{min}\le\lambda_\mathrm{min}\left(T_n^{(2)}(f)\right)\le\lambda_\mathrm{max}\left(T_n^{(2)}(f)\right)\le f_\mathrm{max}.\) (2.8)

## 3. Two Grid method The Galerkin multigrid method belongs to the class of classical multigrid methods and is primarily applicable to symmetric positive definite linear systems _Au=b_. Its simplest form is the two grid method (TGM), which consists of a smoother and a coarse-grid correction. Multi-level schemes such as the V-cycle are realized by recursively cycling the TGM. The specific procedure of the TGM is shown in 1. In this paper, we choose the weighted Jacobi as the smoother, whose update formula is \(u^{(j+1)}=Gu^{(j)}+\omega\mathrm{diag}(A)^{-1}b,\) where _u_(_j_) is the iteration vector at the _j_-th step, and \(G=I_n-\omega\mathrm{diag}(A)^{-1}A.\) (3.1) The coarse grid correction is obtained by combining the restriction operator \(I_h^H\) and the prolongation operator \(I_H^h\), where \(I_h^H\) is a rectangular matrix with full row rank. Specifically, we take \(I_h^H=P\otimes P,\) (3.2) where \(P=\left[\begin{array}{ c c c c c c c } 1 & 2 & 1 & & & & \\ 1 & 2 & & 1 & & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & & \ddots & & \\ & & & 1 & 2 & 1 \end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{[\frac{N}{2}]\times N}.\) The prolongation operator is defined by \(I_H^h=\left(I_h^H\right)^T=P^T\otimes P^T,\) (3.3) which defines a Galerkin coarse matrix \(A_H=I_h^HAI_H^h\). 1) **Pre-smoothing:** Apply _j_1 iterations of _G_ to the system _Au=b_ to obtain _u_(_j_1)
2) **Compute the residual:** _r=b-Au_(_j_1)
3) **Restriction:** \(b_H=I_h^hr\)
4)**Coarse grid equation solving:** Solve the system _AHe=bH_ exactly to obtain \(\hat{e}\)

## 5. Numerical experiments

In Section 3, we discuss the convergence of the TGM. The TGM contains only one coarse level. When the size of the original matrix is too large, the order of the coarse matrix obtained by projection may still be high, and it remains difficult to solve the coarse-grid equation exactly. A natural approach to resolve this difficulty is to recursively apply the TGM on this coarse level to generate coarser levels successively, until the order of the coarsest level is sufficiently small. Except for the coarsest level, each of the remaining grid levels performs only one such recursive procedure, which yields the V-cycle of the multigrid method\[24, 27, 32\].

In this section, we present several numerical experiments to demonstrate the computational efficiency of the multigrid method and verify the acceleration effect of using GPR-predicted parameters on the multigrid solver. Specifically, we set the order of the matrix on the coarsest level of the multigrid method to be no more than 1000. Except for the coarsest level, one weighted Jacobi iteration is applied for pre-smoothing and post- smoothing on all remaining grid levels, and the same input relaxation parameter is used for all weighted Jacobi iterations. In the experiments, we consider three test cases for comparison: the multigrid method with \(\omega=1\) as the relaxation parameter, the multigrid method using GPR-predicted values as the relaxation parameter, and the unpreconditioned conjugate gradient method.

The training strategy of GPR is as follows: starting from _N_=5 with a step size of 5 up to _N_=50, we construct a training set consisting of 10 samples. For each problem size, the quasi-optimal parameter \(\omega\) is obtained via grid search over the interval \[0.001,1\] with a step size of 0.001.For all algorithms, the zero vector is used as the initial iterate, with the stopping criterion

\(\mathrm{RRES}=\frac{\|Au-b\|_\infty}{\|b\|_\infty}\le 10^{-7}.\)

All experiments are carried out using MATLAB (version R2025b) on a laptop equipped with an Intel Core i5-9300H CPU (4 cores, 2.40 GHz) and 8 GB of memory.
